name: Copyright and Trademark for AI Work
title: Copyright and Trademark for AI Work
answer: This page covers how copyright and trademark law applies to work made with or by AI systems, from text-to-image outputs to music and video. It addresses questions of authorship, originality, infringement, and the use of existing trademarks in prompts or outputs. It also tracks disputes over training data and the branding of AI tools themselves.

crumbs.name: Rights and Provenance in AI Art

sections.body: This page covers how copyright and trademark law applies to work made with or by AI systems, from text-to-image outputs to music and video. It addresses questions of authorship, originality, infringement, and the use of existing trademarks in prompts or outputs. It also tracks disputes over training data and the branding of AI tools themselves.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: This reference runs on the site's model and tool registries, which currently list 1000 live image generation models, 1000 video models, 2000 audio models, and 732 AI tools. It also draws on court dockets, copyright office records, and trademark registers. Provenance metadata, such as C2PA or model cards, feeds the rights analysis where available.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is done by reading court filings, registration decisions, and platform policies, then mapping them to specific models and tools. Analysts compare AI outputs with source works to assess similarity, and review prompts and training datasets for evidence of copying or trademark use. Findings are written as neutral summaries of current practice, not as legal advice.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk are tracked through the site's litigation monitor, which currently lists 92 active intellectual property lawsuits, 18 of which involve AI music services. The page records who is suing whom, the legal claims, and the status of each case. It also notes provenance gaps, such as missing training data disclosures or unclear ownership terms in model licenses.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving toward clearer rules on whether AI outputs can be copyrighted and who owns them when a human directs the tool. Courts and registries are likely to set standards for how much human input is enough, and for when training on protected works is fair use. Trademark disputes over AI product names and generated logos are also expected to grow as tools become consumer-facing.
